papers.title_in_file: Quantum-inspired Interpretable Deep Learning Architecture for Text Sentiment Analysis
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, related work, results (accuracy comparison, ablation), conclusion, appendix D; method equations skimmed
papers.what_it_is: A classical deep learning model for text sentiment analysis that borrows quantum mechanics ideas (complex embeddings, density matrices) and is evaluated on five benchmark datasets.

assertions.value: The authors report that their model reaches an accuracy of 80.30 on the MR dataset, 0.5 above the second-best model CE-Mix, and 84.76 on SST, slightly below CICWE-QNN's 85.0.
assertions.anchor: Results on different datasets, main text
quotes: Specifically, our model achieves an accuracy of 80.30 on MR, surpassing the second-best model, CE-Mix, by 0.5.
On SST, our model scores 84.76, which is slightly lower than CICWE-QNN's 85.0
assertions.certainty_reason: Single study, own experiments on five benchmark datasets.
assertions.reader_inference: The model runs on classical hardware; quantum-inspired here is a design analogy, not quantum computation.

assertions.value: The authors state that five binary classification benchmark test sets, taken from an earlier study, are used to evaluate the model.
quotes: Five different binary classification benchmark test sets (Shi et al. 2021) are chosen to evaluate the performance of the proposed model.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own evaluation setup in the Experiments section.

assertions.value: The authors report that test accuracy generally lags behind training accuracy, with noticeable fluctuations on some datasets, which they say indicates potential overfitting.
quotes: test accuracies generally lag behind training, with noticeable fluctuations in datasets like CR and MR, indicating potential overfitting.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical observation from training curves in one study.

papers.title_in_file: Variational methods for solving high dimensional quantum systems
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, section 7 simulation results, section 8 discussion; method sections 2 to 6 skimmed
papers.what_it_is: A numerical comparison of DMRG, restricted Boltzmann machine learning and VQE for ground-state energies of the Fermi-Hubbard and Schwinger models.

assertions.value: The author reports that DMRG reproduced the exact-diagonalization ground state energies of the Fermi-Hubbard model with a very small maximum error and states that DMRG proved successful for both models.
quotes: The maximum error between the DMRG and exact ground state energies is approximately
demonstrating the high accuracy of the DMRG method.
The DMRG algorithm has proven to be successful for these two models
assertions.certainty_reason: Numerical results from one study on two model systems.

assertions.value: The author reports that VQE agreed well with DMRG on the Fermi-Hubbard model but was less accurate, and that its Schwinger model energies were slightly larger than DMRG's.
quotes: The results from VQE show good agreement with those obtained using the DMRG algorithm.
It is worth noting that E0/N obtained by VQE is slightly larger than those obtained by the DMRG algorithm.
the VQE algorithm, although less accurate, is also effective for calculating ground state energies
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulation results from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: VQE results here are for small systems, limited by computation.

assertions.value: The author reports that the restricted Boltzmann machine was reliable only when the interaction strength and system size were not too large, and that it failed to approach the ground state energy of the Schwinger model.
quotes: the results from the restricted Boltzmann machine are reliable when U/t and N are not too large.
the restricted Boltzmann machine is not suitable for solving the Schwinger model as it fails to approach the ground state energy accurately.
assertions.certainty_reason: Negative numerical result from one study.

papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, experiments (tables II, III, VI, VII text), discussion and conclusion
papers.what_it_is: Proposes training quantum pulses directly (VQP) instead of gate parameters (VQC) and tests it on binary classification on pulse simulators and an IBM device.

assertions.value: The authors report that variational quantum pulse learning reached up to 11% and 9% higher accuracy than variational quantum circuit learning on the Qiskit pulse simulators and on ibmq-jakarta, respectively, in a binary classification task.
quotes: VQP learning achieves up to 11% and 9% higher accuracy compared with VQC learning on the qiskit pulse simulators (with system model from real machine) and ibmq-jarkata, respectively
assertions.certainty_reason: Single study, binary classification on small data.

assertions.value: The authors report that a pulse trained on one simulated device and tested on the same device gave 65% accuracy, but 35% when tested on a different simulated device, so VQP is device-dependent.
quotes: if we train on pulse simulator (Lima) and test on pulse simulator (Lima), we can obtain 65% accuracy, but if we train on pulse simulator (Lima) and test on pulse simulator (Quito), the accuracy is only 35%
assertions.certainty_reason: Single measured comparison.

assertions.value: The authors state that VQP learning currently has pitfalls: limited real quantum machine resources and no effective pulse simulator, and the available pulse simulator is not differentiable.
quotes: The current VQP learning has pitfalls, one being the limited resources of the real quantum machine and the other being that we do not have an effective simulator for pulses.
this pulse simulator is not differentiable
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state their own limits in Section VI.

papers.title_in_file: Learnability of a hybrid quantum-classical neural network for graph-structured quantum data
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, section 4 experiments (text), section 5 conclusion; Theorem 1 and appendix not read in detail
papers.what_it_is: Res-HQCNN, a residual quantum neural network trained on graph-structured quantum data, tested in simulation against a universal QNN.

assertions.value: The authors state that, compared with a universal QNN, their Res-HQCNN model performs better at learning graph-structured quantum data, and that graph information improves training and testing results.
quotes: Compared with the universal QNN model, we have shown that our Res-HQCNN model performs better to learn graph-structured quantum data.
the information about graph can bring better training and testing results no matter how many pairs are supervised.
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulated experiments on synthetic data, one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that all quantum states, graphs and labels in their experiments are synthetically or randomly generated with manually defined line or cluster graph topologies, under idealized (noise-free) conditions.
quotes: We note that all quantum states, graphs, and labels used in our experiments are synthetically or randomly generated, with manually defined graph topologies such as line or cluster structures.
Although our current experiments are conducted under idealized conditions
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper's own statement of data and noise scope, Section 5.

assertions.value: The authors report that increased network depth and the use of graph information may lead to higher computational costs.
quotes: These results indicate that both increased network depth and the use of graph information may lead to higher computational costs.
assertions.certainty_reason: Based on recorded running times in one study.

papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, section on quantum advantage, hybrid QGA section, conclusion; other sections skimmed
papers.what_it_is: A survey of quantum genetic algorithms, their fitness and selection steps, and cases of quantum advantage.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that Grover's search as a selection step in Reduced QGAs is the main driver of quantum speedup, and that the Thomson problem encoding is a decisive step toward physical applications.
quotes: We conclude that the encoding used by the Thomson problem is a decisive step toward the use of QGAs in a variety of physical applications, while Grover's search as a selection step in Reduced QGAs is the main driver of quantum speedup.
assertions.certainty_reason: Survey conclusion drawn from reviewed literature, not an own experiment.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing other work, that quantum and hybrid genetic algorithms are not guaranteed to outperform classical ones for every application.
quotes: quantum and hybrid genetic algorithms are not guaranteed to outperform classical ones for every application
assertions.certainty_reason: Cited result, attributed to other work.

assertions.value: The authors report, citing other work, that hybrid QGAs showed a 40% faster convergence rate in Knapsack problems and a 22% reduction in energy consumption for MIMO optimization.
quotes: a 40% faster convergence rate in Knapsack problems via parallel quantum crossover and mutation, a 22% reduction in energy consumption for MIMO optimization using shallow, decoherence-resistant circuits
assertions.certainty_reason: Figures are attributed to cited studies.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing other work, that classical bottlenecks in fitness evaluation and selection can significantly limit quantum speedup potential, particularly for large-scale instances.
quotes: classical bottlenecks in fitness evaluation and selection can significantly limit quantum speedup potential, particularly for large-scale instances
assertions.certainty_reason: Cited statement.

papers.title_in_file: Can Feature Engineering Help Quantum Machine Learning for Malware Detection?
papers.what_it_is: A short preliminary study of feature selection and resampling for quantum classifiers (VQC, QSVM) on the Drebin malware dataset, in simulation and on a 5-qubit IBM machine.

assertions.value: The authors report preliminary results on the Qiskit simulator: a VQC with XGBoost-selected features reached 78.91% test accuracy, and a VQC with decision-tree feature selection reached 62.41%.
quotes: The preliminary results show that VQC with XGBoost selected features can get a 78.91% test accuracy score on 10,000 samples with a 50% test set split.
VQC with DT feature selection got 62.41% test accuracy.
assertions.certainty_reason: Preliminary single-study result on a simulator.

assertions.value: The authors report that on an IBM quantum machine with limited qubits, using 20 samples with a 50% test split, the Quantum SVM got 56% accuracy and VQC got 80% success.
quotes: Due to the limited number of qubits available on the Quantum Machine, we use 20 samples with a 50% test set split.
The Quantum SVM got 56% accuracy and VQC achieved 80% success for malware detection.
assertions.certainty_reason: Tiny sample on real hardware, one study.
assertions.reader_inference: Twenty samples is too few to separate the two classifiers.

assertions.value: The authors state that the practical use of a quantum machine for malware detection is still in its early stages because of physical limitations.
quotes: The practical use of a quantum machine for malware detection is still in its early stages due to the physical limitations.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' own stated limit, Section 6.

papers.what_it_is: A reinforcement-learning agent that chooses sub-problems for Quantum Local Search on random Ising problems, tested in simulation.

assertions.value: The authors report that the RL agent improves the average approximation ratio of Quantum Local Search over random sub-problem selection on fully-connected random Ising problems.
quotes: Our results demonstrate that the RL agent effectively enhances the average approximation ratio of QLS on fully-connected random Ising problems
A noticeable improvement can be observed for the RLQLS compared to the original random sub-problem selection strategy.
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulation results from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that the sub-problem size is set so that quantum solvers with 5 qubits can be employed, and that a Dwave-tabu solver serves as a quantum simulator for the sub-problems.
quotes: so that quantum solvers with 5 qubits can be employed
The Dwave-tabu solver is utilized as a quantum simulator for solving the sub-problems
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper's own statement of setup in Section III.
assertions.reader_inference: No quantum hardware was used for the sub-problems.

assertions.value: The authors state that agent performance was affected by problem size, with smaller rewards for larger problems, and that experiments on real quantum devices are still needed to assess practical applicability.
quotes: smaller episode mean rewards observed for larger problems
conducting experiments on real quantum devices would provide a valuable assessment of the practical applicability of the RL-QLS approach
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' stated limits, Section IV.

papers.title_in_file: A comparison on constrain encoding methods for quantum approximate optimization algorithm
papers.what_it_is: A numerical comparison of three ways of encoding linear constraints in QAOA (QUBO, penalty dephasing, quantum Zeno effect) on the knapsack problem.

assertions.value: The authors state that they numerically compare three strategies for adding linear constraints to QAOA and assess them using the knapsack problem as a case study.
quotes: we conduct a numerical comparison of three different strategies for incorporating linear constraints into QAOA
We assess the efficiency and effectiveness of these methods using the knapsack problem as a case study.
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper's own statement of scope in the Abstract.

assertions.value: The authors report that the QUBO approach needed fewer ancilla qubits and two-qubit gates but more optimization iterations and longer runtimes, and that it struggled with scalability as problem size increased.
quotes: The QUBO approach demonstrated lower quantum resource requirements, such as fewer ancilla qubits and two-qubit gates, but required more optimization iterations and had longer runtimes.
it struggled with scalability as problem size increased.
assertions.certainty_reason: Numerical simulation on one problem type.

assertions.value: The authors report that the quantum Zeno approach, while theoretically promising, met practical challenges from frequent mid-circuit measurements, giving longer runtimes and suboptimal performance.
quotes: The Quantum Zeno effect, while theoretically promising, encountered practical challenges due to the complexity of frequent mid-circuit measurements, leading to longer runtimes and suboptimal performance
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulation result, one problem type.
